title: EXCEPT
description: Learn how to use the EXCEPT operator to subtract the result set of one query from another, returning distinct rows that appear only in the first query.

data.text: SQL Server EXCEPT

Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **EXCEPT**. Learn how to use the EXCEPT operator to subtract the result set of one query from another, returning distinct rows that appear only in the first query. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of EXCEPT and be confident in applying it to your projects.
EXCEPT Syntax

data.title: EXCEPT Syntax
data.content: Returns rows from query_1 that are not in query_2.

data.text: The following are the rules for combining the result sets of two queries in the above syntax:

items: The number and order of columns must be the same in both queries.
The data types of the corresponding columns must be the same or compatible.

data.text: The EXCEPT of two result sets T1 and T2 returns the distinct row(s) from T1 that do not appear in T2.
EXCEPT Examples

data.title: Find Products with No Sales
data.content: Subtract product IDs that have sales from all product IDs.
data.code:
SELECT
    product_id
FROM
    production.products
EXCEPT
SELECT
    product_id
FROM
    sales.order_items;

data.text: In this example, the first query returns all the products. The second query returns the products that have sales. Therefore, the result set includes only the products that have no sales.
EXCEPT with ORDER BY
To sort the result set created by the EXCEPT operator, add the ORDER BY clause to the last query:

data.title: EXCEPT with ORDER BY
data.content: Sort products with no sales by product_id ascending.
data.code:
SELECT
    product_id
FROM
    production.products
EXCEPT
SELECT
    product_id
FROM
    sales.order_items
ORDER BY
    product_id;

data.title: EXCEPT vs NOT IN
data.text: EXCEPT is similar to NOT IN but handles NULL values differently. EXCEPT treats NULL as equal to NULL for comparison purposes, while NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns an empty result set.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: EXCEPT subtracts the result set of the second query from the first query.
It returns distinct rows from the first query not present in the second.
Columns must match in count, order, and compatible data types.
Add ORDER BY to the last query to sort the EXCEPT result set.
EXCEPT is useful for finding differences between two data sets.

data.text: Comprehensive Code Example

This example demonstrates a production-ready implementation of **EXCEPT**. Study the code carefully, paying attention to error handling, type safety, and best practices. Try running it yourself and experiment with variations to deepen your understanding.

data.title: Production-Ready Implementation: EXCEPT
data.content: Complete working example demonstrating best practices and common patterns.
data.code:
-- SQL Example with Best Practices
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    c.email,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders,
    SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spent,
    AVG(o.order_total) AS average_order
FROM 
    sales.customers c
LEFT JOIN 
    sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    AND o.order_date >= DATEADD(year, -1, GETDATE())
WHERE 
    c.is_active = 1
    AND c.created_date >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY 
    c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.email
HAVING 
    COUNT(o.order_id) > 0
ORDER BY 
    total_spent DESC
OPTION 
    (RECOMPILE);

-- Performance Tips:
-- 1. Use appropriate indexes on join columns
-- 2. Avoid SELECT * - specify only needed columns
-- 3. Filter early with WHERE clause
-- 4. Use JOINs instead of subqueries when possible
